benchmark.name: Yudnamutana Copper (sample)
benchmark.domain_scope: Sediment- and structure-hosted copper mineralisation: host-rock control, supergene versus hypogene mineralogy, and the limits of a compiled deposit database
benchmark.description: Small worked example over a real, openly licensed corpus: 34 mineral deposit records from the SA Geodata / SARIG Data Package, filtered to the Yudnamutana Copper district. Every determinate claim carries an evidence locator (MINERAL_DEPOSIT_NO plus column). Three questions only — this is a format demonstration and smoke test, not a full benchmark. See corpus/yudnamutana/ATTRIBUTION.md for licence and attribution.

source_authority.detail: corpus/yudnamutana/*.csv, verbatim rows from the SA Geodata / SARIG Data Package (CC BY 4.0 AU). Field names and values are unmodified, so any claim resolves to MINERAL_DEPOSIT_NO plus column name.
source_authority.note: These are compiled summary records, not primary reports. They faithfully record what the compiler wrote; they are not a substitute for the original company reports, and absences in them are not evidence of absence in the field.

global_variants.note: Carbonate and calc-silicate unit that hosts many deposits in this district.

global_variants.accepted_variants: secondary, oxidised, oxide zone, weathering product
global_variants.note: The corpus flags this as WEATHERING_PRODUCT = Y in mineralogy.csv.

questions.title: Recurring host unit across the district
questions.question: Eleven of the 34 Yudnamutana Copper records name the Wywyana Formation as the host, described variously as marble, limestone, calcareous beds and actinolitic rock. What does this recurrence indicate about the control on copper mineralisation in the district, what second control do the same summaries record, and what does this pattern on its own not establish?
questions.model_answer: The recurrence points to a lithological (stratigraphic) control: the Wywyana Formation is a carbonate and calc-silicate unit, and a chemically reactive carbonate host favours replacement-style copper mineralisation, which is exactly how several of these records describe it (Pinnacles is logged as a replacement deposit in Wywyana marble). The same summaries record a second, structural control acting with it: mineralisation sits on faults, shears and folds rather than being distributed evenly through the unit — Yudnamutana on a fracture system on an anticlinal fold, Mount McDonnell on a local fault within a broader shear zone, Wheal Frost at a faulted contact within the formation. What the pattern does not establish is a genetic model or a source for the copper. A count of host-unit mentions in a compiled database also reflects where people looked and what was mapped, so the concentration is evidence of a favourable host, not proof that the Wywyana Formation controlled ore genesis.
questions.principle: A host unit that recurs across many occurrences signals a favourable chemical or rheological trap, and where that unit is a carbonate the natural reading is reactive replacement. But a favourable host localises mineralisation; it does not by itself explain where the metal came from or how it was transported. Counts drawn from a compiled inventory also carry exploration and mapping bias, so they constrain 'where' far better than 'why'.

gate.pass_condition: The response identifies the recurrence as a lithological or stratigraphic host-rock control, tied to the carbonate or calc-silicate character of the Wywyana Formation. Simply restating that eleven deposits share a host, with no interpretation of why that matters, fails.
fail_examples: States only that the Wywyana Formation is the most common host, without saying what that implies.
Concludes the Wywyana Formation is the source of the copper.
Attributes the recurrence solely to structure and never treats the host lithology as a control.

components.credit_if: The response reads the recurrence as a lithological or stratigraphic control, linked to the carbonate or calc-silicate nature of the host. Naming the replacement mechanism explicitly is credited under C2, not here.

The response identifies the second, structural control recorded in the same summaries (faults, shears, breccia zones, or fold-related fracture systems), and treats it as acting together with the host rather than instead of it. Naming at least one supporting deposit is sufficient but not required.

The response states what the pattern does not establish, 2 points each to a cap of 4: (a) it does not demonstrate a genetic model or metal source, only a favourable site; (b) counts in a compiled inventory carry exploration or mapping bias, so the concentration is not a clean measure of geological preference.

required_concepts: structural control acting with the host
does not establish genesis or metal source

accepted_variants.accepted_variants: metasomatic replacement, carbonate replacement, reactive host replacement

do_not_credit: Concluding the Wywyana Formation is the source of the copper. It is the host; the corpus says nothing about the source. Fails C1.
Treating the eleven mentions as a quantitative measure of prospectivity without acknowledging compilation bias. Does not earn the (b) half of C3.
Asserting a specific deposit model (IOCG, sediment-hosted stratiform, MVT) as established. The corpus does not support attributing one.
Claiming the remaining 23 deposits therefore have no host control; the corpus simply records different or unstated hosts for them.

evidence.claim: Eleven of the 34 district records name the Wywyana Formation in DEPOSIT_SUMMARY.
Pinnacles is described as a replacement deposit in marble of the Wywyana Formation.
Yudnamutana is hosted in actinolitic marble of the Wywyana Formation, in a fracture system on an anticlinal fold.
Mount McDonnell sits on a local fault within a broader shear zone in actinolitic rocks of the Wywyana Formation.
Wheal Frost mineralisation occurs at a faulted contact of quartzite and calcareous beds of the Wywyana Formation.

calibration.response_text: The Wywyana Formation appears as the host in eleven of the thirty-four records, more than any other unit in the district. Other hosts named include the Opaminda Formation, the Bolla Bollana Formation and the Wortupa Quartzite.
calibration.rationale: Gate-fail near miss. The count is accurate and the other hosts are correctly read from the corpus, but the answer never interprets what the recurrence means, which is what the question asks.

calibration.response_text: The Wywyana Formation is a carbonate unit, described as marble and limestone, and carbonate is chemically reactive, so it acts as a favourable host for replacement copper mineralisation. That is why so many of the district's deposits sit in it.
calibration.rationale: Minimum gate pass. The lithological control is identified and correctly reasoned, but the structural control is absent and no limit on the inference is stated.

calibration.response_text: The recurrence indicates a lithological control: the Wywyana Formation is carbonate to calc-silicate (marble, limestone, calcareous beds, actinolitic rock), and a reactive carbonate host favours replacement mineralisation, which is how Pinnacles is explicitly logged. But the deposits are not spread evenly through the unit. The same summaries put them on structures: Yudnamutana on a fracture system over an anticlinal fold, Mount McDonnell on a fault within a shear zone, Wheal Frost at a faulted contact. So a reactive host and structural focusing act together. What this does not show is where the copper came from or by what process, and because these are compiled records the count partly reflects where explorers worked and what has been mapped, so it is evidence of a favourable host rather than proof that the formation controlled ore genesis.
calibration.rationale: Strong response. Both controls identified and linked, and both limits on the inference stated.

questions.title: Supergene versus hypogene copper mineralogy
questions.question: In the district's mineralogy records, malachite, azurite and cuprite are flagged WEATHERING_PRODUCT = Y, while chalcopyrite and bornite are flagged N. Explain the geological distinction this flag records, what it implies about the samples' position relative to depth, and why the ~30% Cu reported for supergene ore at Wheal Gleeson should not be taken as the grade of the deposit at depth.
questions.model_answer: The flag separates secondary minerals formed by weathering from primary minerals that crystallised with the original mineralising event. Malachite, azurite and cuprite are supergene: carbonates and an oxide produced where descending oxidising groundwater attacked primary copper sulphide near surface. Chalcopyrite and bornite are hypogene sulphides, the primary ore. The distinction is therefore a vertical one: the flagged secondary assemblage records the oxidised zone above the water table, and the primary sulphides represent what lies, or lay, beneath the oxidation front. This is why the ~30% Cu recorded for supergene ore at Wheal Gleeson cannot be read as the deposit's grade at depth. Supergene processes dissolve copper from a large volume of rock and reprecipitate it in a narrow enriched zone, so oxide and enriched ore is typically much richer than the primary sulphide that sourced it. The high figure is a weathering artefact as much as a measure of endowment, and the primary grade below has to be established by drilling.
questions.principle: Near-surface oxidation redistributes copper: it is leached from the upper profile and concentrated at and below the water table, so the oxide and supergene zone is not representative of the primary system. Reading a surface or shallow grade as the deposit grade systematically overstates what is there.

gate.pass_condition: The response identifies the WEATHERING_PRODUCT flag as separating secondary or supergene minerals formed by weathering from primary or hypogene minerals of the original mineralisation. Describing the minerals without stating this distinction fails.
fail_examples: Says only that malachite and azurite are green and blue copper carbonates while chalcopyrite is a sulphide, without identifying one set as weathering products.
Reverses the sets, treating chalcopyrite as the weathering product.
Reads the flag as recording sample quality or data reliability rather than a geological origin.

components.credit_if: The response identifies the flag as separating supergene or secondary minerals formed by weathering from primary or hypogene minerals, with the two sets assigned the right way round.

The response links the distinction to depth: the secondary assemblage marks the oxidised zone near surface, typically above the water table or oxidation front, and the primary sulphides lie beneath it.

The response explains why the ~30% Cu supergene figure overstates depth grade, 2 points each to a cap of 4: (a) supergene enrichment concentrates copper leached from a larger volume into a narrow zone, so enriched ore is richer than its source; (b) the primary grade is therefore unknown from this figure and requires drilling beneath the oxidation front to establish.

required_concepts: supergene or secondary versus hypogene or primary
primary grade must be established by drilling

accepted_variants.accepted_variants: base of oxidation, water table, weathering front, redox boundary

do_not_credit: Reversing the two sets, or treating chalcopyrite as a weathering product. Fails C1.

Treating chalcocite as unambiguously supergene. The corpus flags chalcocite both ways in this district (WEATHERING_PRODUCT Y on some records, N on others), which is geologically correct since it forms in both settings.
Concluding that because supergene grades are high, the deposit is economic. That inverts the point of the question.
Claiming the primary grade can be estimated from the supergene grade by a fixed ratio. Does not earn C3.

evidence.claim: Malachite, azurite and cuprite are recorded with WEATHERING_PRODUCT = Y in this district.
evidence.locator: MINERAL in (Malachite, Azurite, Cuprite), column WEATHERING_PRODUCT

evidence.claim: Chalcopyrite and bornite are recorded with WEATHERING_PRODUCT = N and MINERAL_TYPE = ORE.
evidence.locator: MINERAL in (Chalcopyrite, Bornite), columns WEATHERING_PRODUCT and MINERAL_TYPE

evidence.claim: Wheal Gleeson records production of more than 100 t at 30% of supergene ore.
evidence.notes: The summary reads 'Production >100t @ 30% of supergene ore'. The unit on 30% is not spelled out in the record; it is read as per cent copper. The question does not turn on the exact figure.

evidence.claim: Chalcocite appears in the district under both flag values, which is why it is listed as a distractor.
evidence.locator: MINERAL='Chalcocite', column WEATHERING_PRODUCT (both Y and N rows present)

calibration.response_text: Malachite and azurite are copper carbonates and cuprite is a copper oxide, so they are carbonate and oxide minerals. Chalcopyrite and bornite are copper-iron sulphides. The flag therefore records the mineral's chemical class, separating carbonates and oxides from sulphides.
calibration.rationale: Gate-fail near miss. Every mineral is correctly identified chemically, but the flag is read as chemical class rather than weathering origin, so the central distinction is missed.

calibration.response_text: The Y minerals are secondary, formed by weathering of the primary copper sulphides; the N minerals, chalcopyrite and bornite, are the primary hypogene ore.
calibration.rationale: Minimum gate pass. The distinction is correct and the right way round, but nothing is said about depth or about the grade question.

calibration.response_text: The flag separates supergene minerals from hypogene ones. Malachite, azurite and cuprite formed when oxidising groundwater attacked primary copper sulphide near surface, whereas chalcopyrite and bornite are the original sulphides. That makes it a depth distinction: the flagged minerals mark the oxidised zone above the water table, and the primary sulphides sit beneath the oxidation front. It also means the 30% Cu supergene ore at Wheal Gleeson tells you little about grade at depth, because supergene processes strip copper from a large volume of rock and redeposit it in a thin enriched zone, so the enriched ore is far richer than the primary mineralisation that fed it. Establishing the primary grade needs drilling below the base of oxidation.
calibration.rationale: Strong response. Distinction, depth relationship, enrichment mechanism and the drilling requirement are all present.

questions.title: What DEPOSIT_CLASS does and does not record
questions.question: Of the 34 district records, 3 are classed Deposit, 30 Occurrence and 1 Prospect. Wheal Gleeson is classed Occurrence and records production of over 100 t at 30% supergene ore, while Shamrock is classed Deposit and records no production at all. What does this pair show about the relationship between DEPOSIT_CLASS and recorded production, and what can you conclude from this corpus about the criteria behind the classification?
questions.model_answer: The pair shows that DEPOSIT_CLASS is not driven by recorded production. The two records invert the naive expectation: the higher class sits on a record with no production, and a record with substantial historic production carries the lower class. So production history cannot be used to predict or explain the class, and a reader cannot treat Occurrence as meaning 'nothing was ever mined here'. As for the criteria themselves, this corpus does not state them. The tables record the assigned class but contain no definition of Deposit, Occurrence or Prospect and no field explaining why a given record received one. The honest conclusion is that the classification must rest on something outside these tables — most plausibly an assessment of the mineralisation itself rather than of its production history — and that determining the actual rule requires the SA Geodata documentation or vocabulary, not inference from these 34 rows.
questions.principle: A compiled database records the outputs of a classification scheme, not the scheme itself. Where the defining criteria are not in the corpus, the correct move is to establish what the field does not track and say the rule is undetermined, rather than reverse-engineering a plausible-sounding rule from a handful of records.

gate.pass_condition: The response states that DEPOSIT_CLASS is not determined by recorded production, using the inversion in the pair (Deposit with no production, Occurrence with substantial production) as the reason. An answer that explains the class in terms of production, in either direction, fails.
fail_examples: Concludes that Deposit means more was produced and Occurrence means less.
Explains the difference by asserting Shamrock must have had unrecorded production.
Treats the two records as a data-entry error rather than reading what they jointly show.

components.credit_if: The response establishes that class and recorded production are not tied, resting the point on the inversion between the two named records.

The response states that the corpus does not define the classification criteria: no table gives a definition of the classes or a reason for the assignment, so the rule cannot be recovered from these records.

The response draws the practical consequence, either: that 'Occurrence' must not be read as meaning no mineralisation or no historic mining; or that resolving the criteria requires external documentation such as the SA Geodata vocabulary rather than inference from these rows. Either earns the full 3.

required_concepts: class is independent of recorded production
the corpus does not define the classification criteria
the rule cannot be inferred from these records

accepted_variants.accepted_variants: deposit class, the class field, classification field

do_not_credit: Explaining the class by production volume in either direction. Fails C1.

Inventing a criterion (tonnage threshold, resource estimate, drilling density) and presenting it as what the corpus shows. The corpus states no criterion; proposing one as established does not earn C2.
Concluding the database is wrong or internally inconsistent. Nothing here is contradictory once class and production are recognised as independent.
Answering only that more information is needed, with no statement of what the pair does establish. Does not earn C1.

evidence.claim: The district holds 34 records: 3 Deposit, 30 Occurrence, 1 Prospect.
Wheal Gleeson is classed Occurrence and records production of more than 100 t at 30% supergene ore.
Shamrock is classed Deposit and its summary states there are no production records.
No table in the extracted corpus defines the DEPOSIT_CLASS vocabulary or records a reason for an assignment.
evidence.locator: column headers of deposits.csv, mineralogy.csv, commodity.csv, host_lithology.csv
evidence.notes: A negative claim, verified against the four extracted tables only. The full SA Geodata package ships vocabulary files that are not part of this corpus, which is the point the question turns on.

calibration.response_text: Deposit is the highest class, so it marks the most significant mineralisation, with Occurrence below it and Prospect for targets still being tested. Shamrock is a Deposit because uranium was found there in later exploration, which made it more significant than Wheal Gleeson's small historic copper workings.
calibration.rationale: Gate-fail near miss. Fluent, uses real detail from the Shamrock record, and reaches a plausible-sounding ranking — but it invents a criterion the corpus never states and never registers that class and production are independent.

calibration.response_text: The two records show that the class does not follow production: Shamrock is a Deposit with no recorded production, while Wheal Gleeson produced over 100 t and is only an Occurrence. So whatever DEPOSIT_CLASS is tracking, it is not how much came out of the ground.
calibration.rationale: Minimum gate pass. The inversion is read correctly, but nothing is said about the criteria being absent from the corpus or about the practical consequence.

calibration.response_text: The pair breaks any link between class and production: the Deposit record has none, the Occurrence record has over 100 t at 30%. So production cannot explain or predict the class. Beyond that, this corpus does not let you say what the criteria are. None of the four tables defines Deposit, Occurrence or Prospect, and no column records why a given site was assigned its class, so any rule offered would be reverse-engineered from a handful of rows rather than read from the data. The practical consequence is that Occurrence must not be read as 'nothing here' — Wheal Gleeson was mined — and that pinning down the actual criteria needs the SA Geodata vocabulary documentation, which is outside this extract.
calibration.rationale: Strong response. States what the pair establishes, states what the corpus cannot settle, and draws both practical consequences without inventing a criterion.
